title: Wrong but Useful: Bad Answers That Still Help
hook: Multi-agent systems filter messages by how likely they are to be correct. But a wrong answer can carry a good decomposition — and in every model and benchmark tested, wrong-helpful messages showed up.
key_points: Multi-agent pipelines filter messages by agreement, confidence, or automated scores — assuming correct means useful.
Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation caches five messages and replays the same solver with each one visible or hidden.
That replay measures a message's trajectory value: does exposing it help or hurt the downstream reasoning?
Wrong-helpful messages appeared in every benchmark-model combination tested.
Among wrong-answer messages that flipped final correctness, over four in ten flips were helpful.
Passing the complete message worked best; keeping its reasoning beat keeping only its answer.
content_html: When several model instances deliberate, something has to decide which messages shape the final answer. The usual filters — agreement, confidence, automated scores — all encode the same assumption: a message likely to be correct is a message worth keeping. This paper separates those two things and finds they come apart routinely.
extra_html:
The measurement

Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD) is a controlled protocol: cache five independently generated messages, then replay the same downstream solver — the "integrator" — with each message either available or hidden. The difference in outcome is that message's trajectory value: whether exposing it helped or hurt the reasoning that followed. It's a cleaner instrument than asking a judge, because it measures effect rather than perceived quality.

What they found

Across five mathematics and science benchmarks and two openly available model families (gpt-oss-120b and gemma-4-31B-it), wrong-helpful messages appeared in every benchmark-model combination. Among wrong-answer messages that changed final correctness, more than four in ten of those changes were helpful. Controlled repeats indicate the effects aren't replay noise (p=0.0002).

Intervening on the repeatable wrong-helpful cases, the complete message worked best, and retaining its reasoning preserved more success than retaining only its answer — though the authors leave the source of that advantage open. The practical implication is uncomfortable for standard pipelines: a filter that drops everything with a wrong final answer is throwing away decompositions, constraints, and principles the integrator could have used.

related.title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
related.hook: Multi-agent LLM setups help sometimes and hurt other times, with no clear pattern — until you view them as an information bottleneck problem: compressing context helps only when it loses less than it saves.

related.title: Multi-Agent LLMs Fail to Explore Each Other
related.hook: Drop LLM agents into a room together and they don't probe each other's abilities — they lock into narrow, polarized patterns that tank coordination and inflate regret.

related.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
related.hook: Sample the model many times, let each run reason its own way, then take the majority answer - diverse reasoning paths vote out individual errors.

related.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
related.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

flashcards.prompt: What assumption does this paper challenge about filtering multi-agent messages?
flashcards.back_html: That a message likely to be correct is also the message worth keeping. A wrong answer can still contain a useful decomposition, constraint, or scientific principle.

flashcards.prompt: How does Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation measure a message's 'trajectory value'?

choices.text: It caches messages and replays the same solver with each message available or hidden, comparing outcomes
It asks a judge model to rate each message's helpfulness
It measures how often other agents cite the message

flashcards.explanation_html: DHD is a controlled replay protocol: the same integrator solves the problem with a given message visible or hidden, and the difference is that message's trajectory value.

flashcards.prompt: Which form of a wrong-helpful message worked best downstream?

choices.text: The complete message — and keeping its reasoning preserved more success than keeping only its answer
Just the final answer, stripped of reasoning
A one-line summary generated by a separate model

flashcards.explanation_html: The focused intervention found the complete message works best; retaining its reasoning preserves more success than retaining only its answer, though the source of that advantage remains open.
